To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the plume of TCE is being transported along the stream reach by groundwater flow, and that the plume is being diluted and/or attenuated by biodegradation.
a nested monitoring approach is required to delineate groundwater TCE discharge zones in a UK lowland river.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel multi-scale monitoring strategy that can be used in a wide range of lowland stream/aquitard systems to characterise groundwater discharge and its potential impact on the stream environment.
understanding the spatial and temporal dynamics of groundwater discharge and its implications for contaminant transport in a lowland stream.
the identification and characterisation of a TCE plume in a lowland stream/aquitard system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the TCE plume is being discharged to the stream in a highly heterogeneous manner and that the streambed is acting as a significant attenuating zone.

the nested monitoring approach was able to provide a first pass delineation of the TCE plume in the streambed, but that the detailed spatial heterogeneity and potential for biotransformation in the streambed sediments requires a more intensive sampling strategy to provide a definitive understanding of the fate of the plume at this scale.
the streambed is acting as a 'diffusion' barrier to TCE transport, with significant lateral and vertical spatial variation in TCE concentration and the potential for local-scale biodegradation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
nested monitoring approaches are essential in order to characterise the fate of TCE in a streambed at multiple spatial scales.
nested monitoring approaches can be a very effective way of identifying groundwater discharge points and characterising the fate of contaminants at the aquifer-stream interface.

the combination of in-situ streambed diffusion samplings and multi-level drive-point mini-piezo-monitoring provides an effective, cost-efficient and robust approach to delineating the spatial extent and distribution of TCE plumes at multiple spatial scales in the streambed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nested monitoring approach can be a valuable tool for the delineation of contaminant plumes in lowland streams and the identification of the main processes controlling their fate.

nested monitoring approaches are required in order to identify the spatial scale at which the plume interacts with the stream, and that the spatial scale of the plume is not necessarily the same as the spatial scale of groundwater flow in the aquifer.

the use of nested monitoring strategies, which can provide a more detailed picture of the fate of groundwater plumes at the aquifer/river interface, is essential for the accurate delineation of the extent and magnitude of the contaminant threat to aquatic biota.
